\section[outrora]{outrora — formerly, in the old days}

\label{lesson:PT-C274-outrora}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the succession, then the Portuguese for the chronology.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: outrora}
\textbf{outrora} — \textquotedblleft{}formerly, in the old days\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Outrora, esta aldeia tinha muitas crianças.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{In the old days this village had many children.}
\end{quote}

A literary word; \emph{antigamente} is the everyday choice.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{outrora} fuses \emph{outra hora} \textquotedblleft{}another hour, another time\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB lists \emph{hora}), from Latin \emph{alter} \textquotedblleft{}other\textquotedblright{} and \emph{hōra} \textquotedblleft{}hour\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{outrora}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{outrora}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{outrora}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the succession, then the Portuguese for the chronology, then say \emph{outrora} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does outrora mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Formerly, in the old days\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ultimamente]{ultimamente — lately, recently}

\label{lesson:PT-C274-ultimamente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the chronology, then the Portuguese for formerly.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ultimamente}
\textbf{ultimamente} — \textquotedblleft{}lately, recently\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ultimamente tenho dormido mal.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Lately I have been sleeping badly.}
\end{quote}

Often with the \emph{pretérito perfeito composto}: \emph{tenho trabalhado muito}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ultimamente} is built on \emph{último} \textquotedblleft{}last\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{ultimus} \textquotedblleft{}farthest, last\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), with the ending \emph{-mente}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ultimamente}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ultimamente}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{ultimamente}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the chronology, then the Portuguese for formerly, then say \emph{ultimamente} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does ultimamente mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Lately, recently\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[afinal]{afinal — after all, in the end}

\label{lesson:PT-C274-afinal}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for formerly, then the Portuguese for lately.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: afinal}
\textbf{afinal} — \textquotedblleft{}after all, in the end\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Afinal, o exame foi fácil.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The exam was easy after all.}
\end{quote}

Shows that things turned out differently from what you expected. \emph{Afinal, vens ou não?}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{afinal} joins \emph{a} and \emph{final}, which comes from Late Latin \emph{fīnālis} \textquotedblleft{}of the end\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{fīnis} \textquotedblleft{}end\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{afinal}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{afinal}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{afinal}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for formerly, then the Portuguese for lately, then say \emph{afinal} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[gradualmente]{gradualmente — gradually}

\label{lesson:PT-C274-gradualmente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for lately, then the Portuguese for after all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: gradualmente}
\textbf{gradualmente} — \textquotedblleft{}gradually\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A temperatura subiu gradualmente.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The temperature rose gradually.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{gradual}, ‘step by step’.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{gradualmente} is built on \emph{gradual}, a learned word from Medieval Latin \emph{graduālis}, from \emph{gradus} \textquotedblleft{}a step\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gradualmente}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gradualmente}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{gradualmente}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for lately, then the Portuguese for after all, then say \emph{gradualmente} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does gradualmente mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Gradually\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[aos poucos]{aos poucos — little by little, bit by bit}

\label{lesson:PT-C274-aos-poucos}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for after all, then the Portuguese for gradually.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: aos poucos}
\textbf{aos poucos} — \textquotedblleft{}little by little, bit by bit\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Aos poucos, aprendi a nadar.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Little by little I learned to swim.}
\end{quote}

Also \emph{pouco a pouco}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{pouco} is inherited from Latin \emph{paucus} \textquotedblleft{}few, little\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short); \emph{aos} is \emph{a} with the article \emph{os}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{aos poucos}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{aos poucos}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{aos poucos}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for after all, then the Portuguese for gradually, then say \emph{aos poucos} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does aos poucos mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Little by little, bit by bit\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
